summary:
Ezra opens where 2 Chronicles ends, with the same decree: in 538 BC "the LORD stirred the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia" (1:1) to proclaim that the Jewish exiles — the community deported to Babylon when Jerusalem fell in 586 BC — could return and rebuild the temple. The Cyrus Cylinder, a clay inscription from Babylon, documents the policy: Cyrus returned displaced peoples and their gods to their sanctuaries. Some 42,360 go back under Zerubbabel (2:64). They rebuild the altar first, then lay the temple's foundation — and the older priests who had seen Solomon's temple weep so loudly that "The people could not distinguish the shouts of joy from the sound of weeping" (3:13).

Then the work stalls: "the people of the land set out to discourage the people of Judah and make them afraid to build" (4:4), letters go to the Persian court, and construction "remained at a standstill until the second year of the reign of Darius" (4:24) — roughly sixteen years. Preaching restarts it: "the prophets Haggai and Zechariah" (5:1), whose books stand near the end of the Old Testament, stir Zerubbabel and Jeshua to build again; a search of the royal archives turns up Cyrus's decree, Darius orders the work funded from his treasury, and the temple is finished in 516/515 BC (6:15), seventy years after its destruction. Much of this section (4:8–6:18; 7:12–26) is in Aramaic rather than Hebrew — the empire's administrative language — because the book quotes the official correspondence directly.

The book then skips nearly sixty years. In 458 BC — the usual dating, though some scholars place his mission after Nehemiah's, under a later Artaxerxes — Ezra comes up from Babylon, "a scribe skilled in the Law of Moses" (7:6; a scribe was a copyist and teacher of the Law), with a royal letter and treasure for the temple. He refuses an escort for the four-month journey, having told the king that "The hand of our God is gracious to all who seek Him" (8:22). What he finds is intermarriage: people, priests, and Levites (the tribe set apart to serve in the sanctuary) have married into the surrounding peoples — the thing Deuteronomy 7:3–4 warned would turn Israel to other gods. Ezra tears his clothing and prays, "O my God, I am ashamed and embarrassed to lift up my face to You" (9:6); the assembly gathers trembling in heavy rain, and the book ends with the roll of men who sent away their foreign wives and children — no comment or epilogue follows. Ezra and Nehemiah were a single book in Hebrew tradition; the story resumes thirteen years later with Nehemiah.
